title: How to work lazy daisy stitch in cross-stitch
subtitle: Adding detached chain loops as petal or leaf accents
excerpt: Lazy daisy stitch, also called detached chain stitch, forms a small leaf or petal loop on the surface of the fabric. In cross-stitch it is used as an accent detail: a ring of six lazy daisy loops forms a simple daisy flower, and single loops create leaf-shaped accents around a design. Each loop is anchored at its tip with a small straight stitch.
sourceNotes: Lazy daisy stitch used in combination with cross-stitch. Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch and embroidery publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.
A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: Lazy daisy stitch is a loop of
that sits on the surface of the

anchored at its tip. Unlike cross-stitch, lazy daisy is a free-form surface embroidery stitch that is not constrained to the Aida grid. It works on any fabric with a needle that can pierce the surface.
Bring the needle up at the base of where the petal or leaf loop will sit. Mark the tip of the petal with a light pencil mark if the placement needs to be precise.
Insert the needle back into the fabric at the same hole you came up through, or immediately beside it. Do not pull the thread tight; leave a loop of thread lying on the surface.
Bring the needle up through the fabric at the tip of the petal, inside the thread loop. The needle should emerge inside the loop you have formed.
Pull the thread through slowly, letting the loop settle against the fabric in a leaf or petal shape. The loop should lie flat and smooth, not twisted or puckered.

Anchor the tip of the loop with a small straight stitch over the thread at the tip point. Insert the needle just beyond the tip and bring it up at the base of the next petal. The anchor stitch holds the loop shape securely.

items.symptom: The petal loop twists instead of lying flat
items.cause: The loop was pulled tight before it settled into shape, or the thread was twisted as it lay on the fabric.
items.fix: Hold the loop open with a finger as you pull the thread through, and guide it into a flat petal shape before anchoring. Pull slowly and check the loop is untwisted before making the anchor stitch.

items.symptom: The lazy daisy petals are different sizes
items.cause: The length of loop left on the surface before anchoring was not consistent.
items.fix: Mark the tip point for each petal before starting. Bring the needle up at the tip at a consistent distance from the base each time. Consistent needle placement is the key to even petal sizes.

content.text: A six-petal daisy worked around a French knot centre is a classic first lazy daisy project. Position the six petals evenly around the centre point using light pencil marks before stitching. Once the spacing is established, the petals are each a single loop and the whole flower takes only a few minutes.
